docs.title: DocPilot restic documentation
docs.text: These topics document restic, an open-source backup program. They are a sample of a docs-as-code workflow: every topic has a type, a template and automated checks.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• To learn the ideas first, read Repositories and snapshots.
  • To try restic now, follow Install restic.
  • To look up a command, see the Command reference.

docs.title: How this site is organized
docs.text:
Each topic is one of three types:

Type Purpose Concept Explains what something is and why it works that way. Task Gives numbered steps to reach one goal. Reference Lists facts to look up, such as commands and flags.

docs.title: Decision log
docs.text: This log records decisions about how the docs are produced, including what went wrong when AI drafted content and how the review caught it.

docs.title: How to use this log
docs.text: Add one entry each time an AI-assisted draft contains an error. Record the tool, the prompt, the error and the check that caught it. Write only what really happened.

docs.title: Entry template
docs.text: Field Content Date The day you found the error. Tool and prompt The model and the instruction you gave it. What was wrong The incorrect claim, such as an invented flag or an outdated version. How it was caught The check that found it, such as docpilot verify --live. Rule added The new lint rule, checklist item or prompt change.

docs.title: Data handling
docs.text: Use only approved or local AI tools. Never paste confidential or customer data into an unapproved tool. The chatbot in this project refuses to send content to a non-local model unless you pass --allow-remote.

docs.title: Style guide
docs.text: The linter enforces these rules. Run docpilot lint docs before every pull request.

docs.title: Topic types
docs.text: Every topic declares type in its front matter as concept, task or reference. Task topics also record tested_version, the restic version you used when you ran every step.

docs.title: Task topics
docs.text:
• Start with a one-sentence goal.
  • Add a Before you begin section for prerequisites.
  • Put numbered actions under a Steps section.
  • Write one action per step and start it with an imperative verb, such as Run or Create.
  • State what the user should see after a key step.

docs.title: Writing rules
docs.text:
• Keep sentences under 30 words.
  • Use active voice.
  • Remove filler words such as simply, just and please.
  • Give every code block a language tag.
  • Write link text that describes the destination. Never use here.

docs.title: Terminology
docs.text: The file terminology.txt lists words to avoid and the preferred term. The linter reports each match as an error. Examples: use repository, not backup repo, and use use, not utilize.

docs.title: How incremental backups work
docs.text: The first restic backup copies all your data. Later backups are much faster because restic copies only what changed. This topic explains how.

docs.title: Chunks and deduplication
docs.text: Restic splits each file into variable-size chunks and gives every chunk an identifier based on its content. Before it stores a chunk, restic checks whether the repository already has a chunk with the same identifier. If it does, restic skips the copy. This process is called deduplication.

docs.title: What this means for each backup
docs.text:
• The first backup stores every chunk.
  • A later backup reads your files again but stores only new chunks.
  • A renamed or moved file adds almost no data, because its chunks already exist.

docs.title: Every snapshot is complete
docs.text: Although restic stores only changed data, each snapshot describes the full set of files. To restore, you pick one snapshot. You never need to combine a full backup with a chain of smaller ones.

docs.title: Repositories and snapshots
docs.text: Restic stores your backups in a repository and records each backup run as a snapshot. Understanding these two terms makes every other restic task easier.

docs.title: What a repository is
docs.text:
A repository is the location where restic keeps all backup data. It can be a local directory, an external drive, or cloud storage. Restic encrypts everything in the repository with your password.

You choose the repository when you run a command, by using the --repo flag or the RESTIC_REPOSITORY environment variable.

docs.title: What a snapshot is
docs.text:
A snapshot is the state of your files at the moment a backup ran. Each snapshot has a short ID, a time, a host name and the paths it covers.

Restic stores a snapshot as a small record that points to the stored data. You can restore any snapshot completely, even though restic saves only changed data.

docs.title: Why the password matters
docs.text: If you lose the repository password, you cannot recover the data. Restic cannot reset it. Store the password in a password manager.

docs.title: Related topics
docs.text:
• How incremental backups work
  • Create a repository

docs.title: Command reference
docs.text: This topic lists the restic commands used in these docs. Run restic help for the complete list.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: Command Purpose restic init Create a new repository. restic backup Create a snapshot of files and directories. restic snapshots List the snapshots in a repository. restic restore Restore a snapshot to a target directory. restic forget Remove snapshot records, with optional retention rules. restic prune Delete data that no snapshot uses. restic check Verify the repository structure and optionally its data.

docs.title: Common flags
docs.text: Flag Applies to Purpose --repo, -r All commands Path or URL of the repository. --exclude, -e backup, restore Skip files that match a pattern. --target, -t restore Directory to restore into. --keep-last forget Keep the given number of most recent snapshots. --prune forget Delete unused data after forgetting snapshots. --dry-run, -n backup, forget, prune Show what would happen without changing anything. --read-data check Read and verify all stored data.

docs.title: Back up files
docs.text: Create a snapshot of a directory in an existing repository.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text: • Create a repository. This topic uses /tmp/restic-demo-repo.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Create a sample directory that contains one file:

    bash mkdir ~/docpilot-sample echo "hello" > ~/docpilot-sample/notes.txt

  2. Run the backup command:

    bash restic backup ~/docpilot-sample --repo /tmp/restic-demo-repo

  3. Enter the repository password when prompted.

    Restic prints a summary of new and changed files, then snapshot followed by the new snapshot ID and the word saved.

  4. List the snapshots to confirm the backup:

    bash restic snapshots --repo /tmp/restic-demo-repo

    The table has the columns ID, Time, Host, Tags, Paths and Size, and lists one snapshot.

docs.title: Exclude files from a backup
docs.text:
Add the --exclude flag to skip files that match a pattern:

restic backup ~/docpilot-sample --exclude "*.tmp" --repo /tmp/restic-demo-repo

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: Continue with Restore a snapshot.

docs.title: Check a repository
docs.text: Verify that the repository structure is consistent and has no errors.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text: • Create a repository and add at least one snapshot.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Run the check command:

    bash restic check --repo /tmp/restic-demo-repo

  2. Enter the repository password when prompted.

    If the repository is healthy, restic reports that it found no errors.

docs.title: Verify the stored data
docs.text:
By default, check verifies the repository structure but does not read every data file. To read and verify all data, add the --read-data flag. This check can take a long time on large repositories:

restic check --read-data --repo /tmp/restic-demo-repo

docs.title: Create a repository
docs.text: Create an encrypted repository in a local directory.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
• Install restic.
  • Choose a strong password and store it in a password manager. You cannot recover data without it.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Run the initialization command. The command creates the directory if it does not exist:

    bash restic init --repo /tmp/restic-demo-repo

  2. Enter a password when restic prompts you, and enter it again to confirm.

    Restic prints created restic repository, followed by a repository ID and the path you chose. It also warns that losing your password means losing your data.

  3. List the repository directory to confirm that restic created its files:

    bash ls /tmp/restic-demo-repo

    The directory contains a config file and the subdirectories data, index, keys, locks and snapshots.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: Continue with Back up files.

docs.title: Install restic
docs.text: Install the restic command-line program and confirm that it runs.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
• Use macOS, or a Debian-based Linux distribution such as Ubuntu.
  • Make sure you have administrator access on Linux.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Install restic with your package manager.

    On macOS:

    bash brew install restic

    On Ubuntu or Debian:

    bash sudo apt install restic

  2. Check the installed version:

    bash restic version

    The output starts with restic followed by a version number.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: Continue with Create a repository.

docs.title: Remove old snapshots
docs.text: Keep only the most recent snapshots and free the storage that older snapshots used.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
• Create at least four snapshots. Run Back up files several times.
  • Understand that removed snapshots cannot be restored.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Preview the result with a dry run. The dry run changes nothing:

    bash restic forget --keep-last 3 --dry-run --repo /tmp/restic-demo-repo

  2. Review the list of snapshots that restic would keep and remove.

  3. Run the command again without --dry-run, and add --prune to free the storage. Restic reports how many snapshots it removed, and the output ends with done:

    bash restic forget --keep-last 3 --prune --repo /tmp/restic-demo-repo

  4. List the snapshots to confirm that only three remain:

    bash restic snapshots --repo /tmp/restic-demo-repo

docs.title: Forget and prune
docs.text: The forget command removes snapshot records. The prune command deletes stored data that no snapshot uses anymore. The --prune flag runs both in one step.

docs.title: Restore a snapshot
docs.text: Restore the files from a snapshot into a new directory.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text: • Back up files so that the repository contains at least one snapshot.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Restore the latest snapshot to a target directory:

    bash restic restore latest --target /tmp/restic-restore-test --repo /tmp/restic-demo-repo

  2. Enter the repository password when prompted.

  3. List the restored files:

    bash find /tmp/restic-restore-test -name notes.txt

    Restic recreates the original directory path inside the target directory, so the file appears under that path.

docs.title: Restore a specific snapshot
docs.text:
Replace latest with a snapshot ID from the output of restic snapshots:

restic restore 1a2b3c4d --target /tmp/restic-restore-test --repo /tmp/restic-demo-repo
